narrative_purpose: Shows why the convenient 26-hour clock fails physically: an Earth-sized moon orbiting a Jupiter-sized planet that quickly must skim close enough to be violently flexed and heated, unlike a wider habitable orbit.
subject: Two equal side-by-side views of the same banded gas giant and the same blue-green moon. On the left, the moon skims extremely close above the giant's cloud tops; its globe is visibly stretched toward the planet and crossed by many hot orange volcanic fissures, with a plume erupting from the near side. On the right, the moon sits several planet radii farther away; it remains round, blue-green, ocean-bearing and only faintly warm inside, with no erupting fissures. The gas giant is the same size in both panels for comparison.
scene: Deep space around Polyphemus, contrasting the tight day-long orbit required by canon with a wider orbit that a habitable large moon could survive.
camera: Flat side-on astronomical comparison, matched scale and viewing angle in both halves.
light: Cool distant starlight on both; the close moon adds fierce ember-orange internal heat, while the wider moon carries only a soft cyan atmospheric rim.
palette: Global void-indigo and muted cream-rust planet bands; scarce but intense ember heat on the close moon, living teal and cyan on the wider moon.
style: Painterly comparative astronomy plate with tactile planetary surfaces, not a vector orbital chart.
detail_level: Crisp moon shapes and fissures; planet bands slightly softer; plain dark background for later labels.
composition: Matched halves with gas giant on the inner edge and moon outward; the left gap extremely narrow, the right gap visibly several times wider.
consistency_notes: Both panels show the same Polyphemus and same moon at different orbital distances. The close case must read as distorted and volcanically overheated; the wide case as round and habitable.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no orbit rings, no arrows, no planet-size mismatch between panels, no extra moons, no photographic or 3D-render look, no lens flares
